items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that Bobby and his dad took a [MATH: 2]-hour car trip from Boston to Rochester. The car was traveling at a constant speed, and they traveled [MATH: 70] miles.

Content:
We can represent this information visually using a distance-time graph, where distance is plotted as a function of time. To construct the distance-time graph, we use the given information to find two points on the graph.

Content:
- At time [MATH: t=0,] the distance they had traveled was [MATH: 0] miles. So, our graph will start at the point [MATH: (0,0).]
- We also know that it took them [MATH: 2] hours to travel [MATH: 70] miles, so our graph will pass through the point [MATH: (2,70).]

Content:
Now, we plot these two points and connect them to form a line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e4e7ce520045b45917d2dc284e1c0b12]

Content:
This is our distance-time graph! Its slope represents the speed of the car:

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac{70 - 0 }{2- 0 } = 35]

Content:
The units of speed are units of distance (miles) divided by units of time (hours). Therefore, the speed of the car is [MATH: 35\, \textrm{miles/hour}.]

Content:
We can also use the slope to write the equation of the line. In slope-intercept form, the line can be written as

Content:
[MATH: s = mt + b.]

Content:
We know that the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: b=0] and the slope is [MATH: m=35.] So, the equation of the line is
[MATH: s = 35t+0,]
or more simply,
[MATH: s = 35t.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The slope of the distance-time graph gives the speed. So, to compute the speed of the cyclist, we need to find its slope.

This line begins at [MATH: (0,1)] and also contains the point [MATH: (2,7).] So, we can find the speed by computing the slope as follows:

[MATH: m|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (7meters − 1meter)/(2seconds − 0seconds); = 3meters/second]

Therefore, the speed of the cyclist was [MATH: 3\,\textrm{m/s}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that Bobby and his dad took a [MATH: 2]-hour car trip from Boston to Rochester. The car was traveling at a constant speed, and they traveled [MATH: 70] miles.

Content:
We can represent this information visually using a distance-time graph, where distance is plotted as a function of time. To construct the distance-time graph, we use the given information to find two points on the graph.

Content:
- At time [MATH: t=0,] the distance they had traveled was [MATH: 0] miles. So, our graph will start at the point [MATH: (0,0).]
- We also know that it took them [MATH: 2] hours to travel [MATH: 70] miles, so our graph will pass through the point [MATH: (2,70).]

Content:
Now, we plot these two points and connect them to form a line.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/e4e7ce520045b45917d2dc284e1c0b12]

Content:
This is our distance-time graph! Its slope represents the speed of the car:

Content:
[MATH: m = \dfrac{70 - 0 }{2- 0 } = 35]

Content:
The units of speed are units of distance (miles) divided by units of time (hours). Therefore, the speed of the car is [MATH: 35\, \textrm{miles/hour}.]

Content:
We can also use the slope to write the equation of the line. In slope-intercept form, the line can be written as

Content:
[MATH: s = mt + b.]

Content:
We know that the [MATH: y]-intercept is [MATH: b=0] and the slope is [MATH: m=35.] So, the equation of the line is
[MATH: s = 35t+0,]
or more simply,
[MATH: s = 35t.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Speed of an Object

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/e35b05c450c1ec67a6b94b639642b984]

The graph above shows the distance traveled by a cyclist on a road over a period of [MATH: 4] seconds. What was the speed of the cyclist?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The slope of the distance-time graph gives the speed. So, to compute the speed of the cyclist, we need to find its slope.

This line begins at [MATH: (0,1)] and also contains the point [MATH: (2,7).] So, we can find the speed by computing the slope as follows:

[MATH: m|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (7meters − 1meter)/(2seconds − 0seconds); = 3meters/second]

Therefore, the speed of the cyclist was [MATH: 3\,\textrm{m/s}.]
